title: From Next-Token Prediction to Capabilities
subtitle: AI Course 2026 — Module Q01 companion video

slides.title: The question
bullets: How does predicting the next token produce problem solving, coding, and instruction following?
The objective sounds trivial — the behavior does not
slides.narration: How does next-token prediction lead to problem solving, coding, and instruction following? This is the central puzzle of modern language models. The training objective sounds almost trivial: guess the next word. Yet the behavior that emerges from it includes writing working code, following complex instructions, and solving multi-step problems. In this video we unpack the standard answer: prediction as compression, in-context learning, scale, and post-training. Four ideas, one story.

slides.title: What the training objective actually is
bullets: Given a prefix, output a probability distribution over the next token
Cross-entropy loss rewards calibrated predictive accuracy
Everything else is emergent from this single signal
slides.narration: First, let us be precise about the objective. A language model takes a prefix of text and outputs a probability distribution over the next token. Training exposes the model to enormous amounts of text and adjusts its parameters to minimize cross-entropy loss: the negative log probability the model assigns to the actual next token. That is all. There is no module for coding, no module for reasoning, no objective that mentions instructions. Everything that interests us is emergent from this one signal.

slides.title: Tokens, not words
bullets: Byte-pair encoding splits text into subword units
A vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens
Next-token prediction operates over this vocabulary
slides.narration: A note on vocabulary. Models predict tokens, not words. Text is split by a byte-pair encoding tokenizer into subword units from a fixed vocabulary of typically fifty to a hundred thousand entries. Common words are single tokens; rarer words split into pieces. This matters because the model must learn the statistics of these units, and the choice of tokenization shapes what patterns are easy or hard to learn.

slides.title: Prediction is compression
bullets: To predict well, the model must model the process that generated the text
Cross-entropy is code length: minimizing loss is compression
Shannon's source coding view of language modeling
slides.narration: The first big idea: prediction is compression. To assign high probability to text, you must model the process that generated it. Code that solves a problem is generated by reasoning about the problem. Instructions are written by intentional humans following conventions. Proofs are generated by chains of logic. A predictor that compresses all of this well must internalize something about the generating processes themselves. Formally, cross-entropy is expected code length under the model, so minimizing loss literally minimizes the number of bits needed to encode the corpus. Good prediction and good compression are the same thing.

slides.title: Why compression forces internal models
bullets: Randomness cannot be predicted — the irreducible part
Everything non-random in text comes from structure: syntax, facts, logic, style
The cheapest sufficient statistics of text are models of its causes
slides.narration: Why does compression force internal models? Because the only way to spend fewer bits on text is to exploit its regularities. Syntax is regular. Facts are consistent. Logic is rigid. Style is coherent across a document. A model that captures these regularities spends bits only on the genuinely unpredictable residue. The cheapest representation of a regularity is, in effect, a model of the process that produced it. That is why a good next-token predictor of code, dialogue, and proofs must contain machinery that behaves like an understanding of code, dialogue, and proofs.

slides.title: In-context learning
bullets: Give examples in the prompt; the model continues the pattern
No gradient updates — the behavior is in the forward pass
GPT-3 paper: few-shot learning without fine-tuning
slides.narration: The second big idea is in-context learning. Put a few solved examples of a task inside the prompt, and a large model will solve new instances of that task, with zero weight updates. The GPT-3 paper made this famous: models performed translation, question answering, and arithmetic patterns described only by examples in the context. Nothing in training explicitly optimized for this. It tells us the pre-trained network implements general pattern-completion machinery, and that a capability can live entirely in the forward pass.

slides.title: Why in-context learning is possible at all
bullets: Training data contains documents that are themselves pattern-completions
Tables, exercises with answers, code with comments, dialogs
The model learns the meta-pattern: continue the established format
slides.narration: Why is this even possible? Because the training corpus is full of documents that are themselves pattern-completions: tables with consistent columns, exercise sets with answers, code files where functions follow the naming style, question-answer dialogs. A model that compresses such documents well must learn the meta-pattern: within a document, continue the established format. In-context learning is that meta-pattern, repurposed at inference time. The prompt is a temporary document, and the model completes it.

slides.title: Instruction following from next-token prediction
bullets: Instruction-response pairs exist in the wild (forums, docs, Q&A)
Pre-training already sees 'here is a request, here is a compliant response'
Post-training amplifies this into reliable behavior
slides.narration: How does instruction following arise? The corpus is not just prose. Forums, documentation, and question-answer sites contain millions of request-response pairs where a human states a task and another human complies. A model compressing these learns the conditional distribution of compliant responses given requests. The raw pretrained model does this unreliably. Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback then select and amplify the compliance behavior. Pre-training provides the raw capability; post-training makes it dependable.

slides.title: Coding from next-token prediction
bullets: Code is the most regular, most compressible text we produce
Compilation and tests provide natural verifiers
The model learns both surface syntax and solution patterns
slides.narration: And coding? Code is the most regular text humans produce: rigid syntax, strong naming conventions, repeated architectural patterns, and entire ecosystems of similar solutions. It compresses extremely well, so a model trained on enough code necessarily internalizes syntax and solution patterns. Moreover, code comes with natural verifiers: it compiles or it does not, tests pass or fail. That verifiability is exactly what later reinforcement learning stages exploit to sharpen coding ability far beyond what imitation alone gives.

slides.title: Why scale changes the picture
bullets: More parameters and data mean sharper internal models
Loss follows smooth power laws in compute, data, parameters
Some abilities appear abruptly; whether that is real is debated
slides.narration: The third big idea is scale. Empirically, loss falls along smooth power laws as you grow parameters, data, and compute. But downstream abilities do not always improve smoothly: certain benchmarks jump from near-random to strong performance across a relatively narrow range of model sizes. These are the so-called emergent abilities. A lively debate asks whether the thresholds are real properties of the models or artifacts of discontinuous metrics. Either way, the practical fact stands: the internal models learned by prediction become qualitatively more useful with scale.

slides.title: Generalization versus memorization
bullets: The model cannot store the whole internet verbatim
Compression prefers reusable structure over rote tables
Evidence: performance on unseen problems and held-out data
slides.narration: Is all this just memorization? No model has enough parameters to store its training corpus verbatim. Under a compression pressure, reusable structure is cheaper than rote tables: learning the rules of arithmetic costs fewer bits than memorizing every arithmetic statement ever written. And empirically, models solve problems constructed after their training cutoff and handle novel combinations of familiar ideas. Memorization certainly happens, especially for rare strings. But the interesting capabilities come from the learned structure.

slides.title: The counterpoint: what prediction does not explain
bullets: Confident errors and hallucination follow from the same objective
Prediction of plausible text is not the same as truth-tracking
Hence the need for retrieval, verifiers, and post-training
slides.narration: For balance: the same account explains the failure modes. A model optimized for plausible text will produce plausible-sounding falsehoods when truth is not the cheapest pattern to learn. Hallucination, sycophancy, and confident mistakes are not bugs bolted onto an otherwise honest system; they are what pure next-token prediction does when the corpus itself is inconsistent or when the truth is underrepresented. The mitigations — retrieval, tool use, verification, preference training — all work by changing what the model conditions on or what it is rewarded for.

slides.title: What we can measure: perplexity and bits per token
bullets: Perplexity = effective branching factor of the model
Bits per token makes compression literal
These are the meters on the training dashboard
slides.narration: What does the compression story look like on a training dashboard? Perplexity is the exponentiated average loss: roughly, the effective number of equally likely next tokens the model is deciding among. Lower perplexity means sharper prediction. Bits per token is the same number expressed as code length. When you read that a frontier model achieves, say, under one bit per token on web text, that is the compression view made concrete: the model has found a lot of structure.

slides.title: A worked micro-example
bullets: Bigram model: predict from the previous token only
Neural model: condition on the whole context
Watch the same objective produce qualitatively different behavior
slides.narration: A micro-example makes this concrete. A bigram model implements next-token prediction by counting: it looks only at the previous token and outputs observed frequencies. It is a legitimate language model, and it is helpless beyond local statistics. A neural model implements the same objective but conditions on the entire context through learned representations. The objective is identical; the architecture determines how much structure the model can exploit. The module tutorial walks this gradient in code, from counting to attention.

slides.title: Post-training in one picture
bullets: SFT: imitate curated demonstrations
Preference optimization: RLHF, DPO
RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning: RLVR, GRPO
slides.narration: Post-training deserves one clean picture. Supervised fine-tuning imitates curated demonstrations of good behavior. Preference optimization, whether RLHF with a reward model or direct preference optimization, pushes the model toward responses humans prefer. And for domains with checkable answers, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains reasoning chains directly on correctness. Each stage assumes the pre-trained capability exists and works to surface, select, or sharpen it. None of them creates competence from nothing.

slides.title: Is it intelligence? the honest boundary
bullets: Behavioral capabilities are real and measurable
Whether prediction constitutes understanding is open
This module's claim is mechanistic, not philosophical
slides.narration: A boundary note. Everything in this video is a mechanistic claim: prediction plus scale plus post-training produces these behaviors, and we can trace why. Whether that constitutes intelligence, or understanding, or something else entirely, is a philosophical question that the next module takes up directly. What we can say here is narrow and defensible: the behaviors students care about, problem solving, coding, instruction following, arise from a training signal that never mentions any of them.

slides.title: Open questions at the frontier
bullets: How faithful are chain-of-thought explanations?
Where exactly do capabilities live in the weights?
Does the recipe keep working past the data wall?
slides.narration: Three open questions frame the frontier. First, when a model explains its reasoning in words, is that the computation it actually performed? Evidence on chain-of-thought faithfulness is mixed and is its own module. Second, interpretability research is mapping where specific facts and behaviors live in the weights, with early but striking results. Third, the recipe depends on ever more data, and high-quality text is finite; synthetic data and reinforcement learning are the current answers. Each question has its own module in this course.

slides.title: How to read this topic's literature
bullets: The compression view: Shannon, and the language-modeling-as-compression line
Emergence and its critics; scaling laws papers
In-context learning: the GPT-3 paper and the Bayesian-adapter debate
slides.narration: If you want to go deeper, the reading paths are clear. For the compression view, start with Shannon's 1951 prediction of English, then the modern language modeling is compression results. For emergence, read the original emergent-abilities paper and its mirage critique together. For in-context learning, the GPT-3 paper is the primary source, followed by the literature on whether in-context learning implements implicit Bayesian inference. The module bibliography has full citations and reading order, and the discussion questions are designed for seminar debate.

slides.title: Recap
bullets: Prediction = compression of the generating processes behind text
In-context learning: capability in the forward pass, no updates
Scale sharpens the internal models; post-training steers them
The story explains failures as well as successes
slides.narration: To recap. Next-token prediction is compression, and compression forces internal models of the processes that generate text. In-context learning shows those models acting in a single forward pass. Scale sharpens them, and post-training steers them into reliable assistants. And the same story explains the failures: plausible falsehoods are what pure prediction produces when truth is not the cheapest pattern. For worked examples, the survey evidence, and runnable code, see the full module tutorial and the Beamer deck.
